name: Hitchens's Razor
statement: What can be asserted without evidence can be dismissed without evidence.
meaning: If someone advances a claim but offers no evidence or argument for it, you are under no obligation to construct a rebuttal. A bare assertion can be met with a bare rejection.
mechanism: The razor rests on the burden of proof: the duty to justify a claim lies with the person making it, not with the person doubting it. If that duty is never discharged, the claim earns no rational credence, and the doubter need not mount a positive case to set it aside. The symmetry is the engine — evidence-free assertion licenses evidence-free denial. Crucially, it does not show the claim is false; it shows that none of your effort is owed to it until support arrives.

examples.text: Someone insists an invisible, undetectable dragon lives in their garage and offers nothing testable. The razor says you may set the claim aside without producing counter-evidence — the burden was theirs, and they never met it.
A claim built so that no possible observation could count against it supplies no evidence by construction. Under the razor it can be declined rather than laboriously refuted.
Hitchens deployed it chiefly against assertions of the divine: an existence claim advanced without supporting evidence, he held, may be declined without the sceptic building a positive disproof.

variants.name: The Sagan standard
variants.text: 'Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence' (Carl Sagan). The complement to the razor: it scales the evidence demanded to how implausible the claim is.

variants.name: Russell's teapot
variants.text: Bertrand Russell's analogy of an undetectable teapot orbiting the Sun: the burden of proof lies with the one asserting the teapot, not with the doubter who declines to believe in it.

whyItMatters: It is a rule for allocating argumentative effort. Without it, any claimant can force endless work simply by asserting things; with it, the labour stays where it belongs — on whoever wants you to believe something. It keeps a debate honest about who owes the evidence.

working.lead: Put the burden back on the claimant
working.text: when a claim arrives without support, ask for the evidence rather than supplying its refutation; the duty to justify is theirs.
an unsupported assertion earns a withholding of belief, not a full counter-case; spend your effort on claims that actually offer something to engage.

working.lead: Scale your demand to the claim
working.text: pair it with the Sagan standard — the more extraordinary the assertion, the more evidence it must carry before it earns a hearing.

limits: The razor governs burden of proof and rational credence, not truth: dismissing a claim as unsupported does not prove it false, and an unproven claim may still turn out to be true — absence of evidence is not always evidence of absence. Its main failure mode is misuse, waving away a claim that in fact has evidence which simply was not cited in the moment, so that a rule about unsupported assertions becomes a lazy conversation-stopper. It tells you what you must argue, not what is the case.
misreadings: It is not a proof that unevidenced claims are false — only that they earn no belief until evidence is given. Nor is it licence to ignore evidence when it does appear; the razor applies to bare assertions, and dissolves the moment a claim is actually supported.
origin: Attributed to the writer Christopher Hitchens, who put it in his 2007 book God Is Not Great and used it mainly against religious claims. The idea is much older — a restatement of the classical burden-of-proof maxim 'quod gratis asseritur, gratis negatur' ('what is asserted without reason may be denied without reason') — and the name 'Hitchens's razor' was popularised after his death in 2011.

sources.text: Hitchens, C. (2007). God Is Not Great: How Religion Poisons Everything. Twelve. — the sentence appears at p. 258.
